We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create associated interpolating currents, and compute their masses, decay constants, and production rates through QCD sum rules. Utilizing current algebra, we then determine their relative production ratios in $\Lambda_b^0$ decays. The study also examines their decay properties and applies the Fierz rearrangement to analyze their ratios in the $J/\psi p$ mass spectrum. The findings indicate that $\bar D^{*} \Omega_c$ and $\bar D \Xi_c^*$ could be molecular states with distinct properties, whereas the remaining states exhibit similar characteristics, leading to a complex scenario, where most of these hadronic molecular states may exist simultaneously. Finally, we discuss their potential observations in future experiments.

Encouraging students to learn critical software development skills, such as testing, can be a challenge even with rewards and penalties.  A possible solution lies in teaching these concepts within a fun, interactive learning environment that fosters student inquiry and exploration.  In this paper, we report on an innovative approach to teaching testing principles to high school students through a recently developed educational game, "Debugging for Dummys".  The game's core idea is built around a simple simulation of a fantasy world where students take on the role of wizards, tasked with fixing problems in their community by writing test cases.  A preliminary study with 25 students, implemented as an after-school program, aimed to identify the most effective game design elements and understand students' learning experiences.  Our results indicate that students generally enjoy the game and consider it an effective tool for learning.  Moreover, we have identified several key insights that will guide the game's further development and provide valuable insights for educators on how to structure their teaching practices to best take advantage of inquiry-based learning. Domain adaptation has numerous applications across various fields but is limited by current methods that often rely on large amounts of labeled data. A new approach, semi-supervised mutual enhancement, is presented by two domain adaptation techniques: semi-supervised learning and mutual exclusion. By combining these methods, a framework is developed that not only utilizes a limited number of labeled targets but also excludes redundant information in features, leading to improved performance. This is achieved through a cycle gradient penalty that enforces the exclusion of redundant information in adapted sources and target networks. Furthermore, a novel loss function is proposed, semi-supervised contrastive loss, that retains target information while promoting discriminative features in adapted networks. Experiments on adapted semantic segmentation and adapted image classification show that the proposed method, sSME, outperforms existing domain adaptation techniques by a significant margin, improving performance by up to 17% on the adapted semantic segmentation dataset cross-city, and outperforming state-of-the-art methods by 4% on the adapted image classification dataset cross-sensory. sSME also demonstrates superior robustness to target label noise compared to existing domain adaptation methods. sSME's source code and models will be publicly available.

This text offers an in-depth explanation of the theoretical underpinnings of variable instantiation in Answer Set Programming. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using (fixed) variable instantiation. Specifically, we explore the concept of well-established operators to facilitate a step-by-step processing of grounding algorithms and provide a calculus for deriving answer sets based on these processed results. Furthermore, we introduce a notion of grounding completeness and demonstrate its application to different classes of ASP programs. Ultimately, this work lays the foundation for future analyses of various grounding algorithms and variable instantiation techniques within the ASP framework. Novel view synthesis has seen significant advancements through the utilization of light field synthesis techniques, particularly for scenes with unobstructed views and sufficient image coverage. However, real-world scenes typically have obstructed views, necessitating the estimation of unseen views, a task better handled by deep learning-based methods. These deep learning-based methods, led by models such as MLPs, LNFs, and MAF, have made notable improvements by leveraging four-dimensional light field representations. However, their success is often limited by their high computational requirements, massive memory needs, and restricted generalizability to scenes with varied subject motions. In contrast, our proposed four-dimensional light field representation-based model, SDP-MLP, strikes a balance between performance and efficiency, making it more suitable for real-world applications. Utilizing a four-dimensional representation and distilling knowledge from Meso-MLPs, our model achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis performance at a fraction of the computational cost and memory needs. Furthermore, our model's ability to accurately predict sparse views enables the creation of complete four-dimensional light field reconstructions from sparse data, a capability not previously demonstrated. Extensive evaluations using benchmark datasets showcase the superior view quality produced by our proposed model, particularly when given access to only a few known views. The Scorer equation describes a closed system of non-linear equations for the statistical properties of vorticity, and is derived from the Navier-Stokes equations through a Hamiltonian approximation. The equation features a notable duality between its forward and reverse time solutions, and its Hamiltonian structure allows for the identification of conserved quantities. The study demonstrates that by focusing on specific forms of exact invariant solutions to the Scorer equation, it is possible to obtain scaling laws for random vortex distributions that are relevant to the three-dimensional Euler equation. The research highlights the utility of random vortex dynamics as a statistical model of conservative fluid dynamics, and provides a fundamental framework for understanding hydrodynamic turbulence. Boson sampling has been a prominent system-in-a-box experiment, showcasing interesting phenomena resulting from the interference of numerous bosons. To gain a deeper understanding of this system, we investigate its entropy. Prior studies have demonstrated systems to reach maximum entropy when the sampling rate equals the system's dimension, $\chi$. Our research reveals that this maximum entropy is proportional to the number of modes, $N$, when each mode is occupied by an average of $\mu$ bosons. Specifically, the optimal entropy is found to be $N\mu\left(1-{\rm exp}\left(-\mu\right)\right)$. To verify this, we conduct a simulation to assess the accuracy of an entropy estimator in a system of 14 photons on 14 modes within an average boson number range of 1 to 6. Our findings confirm that the estimated entropy reaches its highest at $\mu=5.55$ before decreasing, substantiating the claim that entropy is a function of $N$ and $\mu$. Furthermore, the relationship between entropy and $\mu$ displays non-linear characteristics, similar to the behavior observed in Shannon entropy, providing a means to compare different boson sampling experiments. These findings open the door for utilizing this entropy estimator to analyze and compare various experimental setups. Moreover, the estimated entropy may serve as a useful indicator of the interference properties of a system during an experiment. Ultimately, the concept of entropy offers a valuable tool for evaluating and analyzing quantum systems in a system-in-a-box framework. To explore this further, we investigate the effects of entanglement on the entropy of a system and compare it with the entropy generated by a product state. Our analysis reveals that the maximum achievable entropy in a product state is significantly lower than the entropy in an entangled system, illustrating the importance of entanglement in this system. To compare these different types of states, we utilize the entanglement measure, $E$, which we found to be directly related to the estimated entropy when the entanglement measure is near its maximum, indicating that the estimated entropy can serve as an indicator of entanglement in a system. Ultimately, the estimated entropy may serve as an essential tool for evaluating and analyzing quantum systems in a system-in-a-box framework by providing insight into the system's interference properties and entanglement properties. In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from a particular frame or a short sequence. However, real-world actions typically possess distinct spatial and temporal characteristics. For instance, breaking glass might start with a focal point over all time frames but possesses strong spatial features near the boundaries, whereas kicking a ball may begin with a focus on the ball itself, accompanied by varying degrees of spatial and temporal features throughout the kick. Most existing models struggle to model these intricate relationships between spatial and temporal features. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel model called OTRF-Net that captures the intricate dependencies between spatial and temporal features in action data. Specifically, OTRF-Net consists of a Transformer-Net that aggregates temporal information and a Object-Relation-Driven Net that integrates spatial features to produce a comprehensive representation of the action. We conduct a series of ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of our model and evaluate its performance on conventional action datasets, achieving superior performance compared to existing models. Moreover, we introduce a new spatiotemporal action dataset, KITTI-Flow, to better capture the nuances of real-world actions. Our model also outperforms existing models on this new dataset. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the increased use of deep learning-based solutions may be counterproductive in this context, as it leads to overfitting and decreased robustness. Ultimately, the results of the competition highlight the difficulty of accurately identifying exact image copies, especially through transformations like cropping, and indicate that the problem is far from fully solved yet. The equation features a contact boundary condition represented by the gradient of a free energy function, \(\nabla\varphi(\zeta)\), where \(\zeta\) is a diffusion target variable and the interaction is coupled with a small parameter \(\varepsilon\) characterizing the scale of perturbations. The metastability effects become significant when this parameter approaches zero and our analysis focuses on the behavior of the equation as \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero. The equation is scaled in the spatial and temporal domains by the parameters \(\varepsilon^{\beta}\), \(\veta^{\alpha}\), and \(\omega^{\delta}\), leading to the identification of three regimes based on the relationships between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The regime corresponding to \(\alpha = 2\) and \(\beta = 1\) is analyzed through the mean exit time of a stochastic process, while the case of \(\alpha = 0\) and \(\beta = 1/2\) is investigated using the mean squared displacement of the mean zero part of the target variable \(\zeta\). Our findings demonstrate that very strong magnetic fields can induce substantial spin polarization in nuclear matter and its various extensions, while the associated symmetry energy and resulting quasiparticle energy gap exhibit a direct correlation with the magnetic field strength. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated an error-correcting code that utilizes the rank of tensors to limit information leakage. This method provides proven guarantees for the privacy of individual data samples and overall data sets. Moreover, we demonstrate its practical benefits in the context of federated learning by achieving faster convergence times while maintaining higher accuracy on real-world datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100) compared to non-private training. The source code is available on the repository https://github.com/ashishanagpal/dpcqc under an MIT license. Our study contributes to the understanding of how our approach impacts the privacy of individual data samples and the privacy of the entire dataset. The experimental results reveal that as the degree of differential privacy increases, the proposed algorithm converges faster and achieves higher accuracy, while maintaining a more efficient communication pattern that is less influenced by differential privacy. The length of the communication channel remains nearly the same regardless of the differential privacy parameter. Moreover, we found that in the absence of differential privacy constraints, our approach yields significantly reduced communication costs, up to 2.9 times lower, without any privacy constraints. This outcome is due to the fact that our method uses a code that can be decoded even when there is no privacy, leading to substantial communication savings. The proposed algorithm's performance compares favorably to a recent model that combined differential privacy with vectorized gradient compression. Specifically, our method achieves faster convergence times (on the order of 1.8-2.1 seconds) while maintaining higher accuracy (up to 1.1% higher top-1 accuracy on CIFAR10 and 1.1% higher top-1 accuracy on CIFAR100). A comprehensive far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectral energy distribution has been created for the Taurus-Aurigae dark cloud complex, thanks to new GALEX observations and a revised extinction map. This SED shows that the FUV continuum emission can be primarily attributed to dust scattering of starlight, both within the dark cloud and in the surrounding regions. To further understand the FUV spectral energy distributions, extinction maps have been updated to pinpoint the locations of very low luminosity objects (VLOs), including young stellar objects (YSOs). It's found that the FUV luminosity associated with these objects, including YSOs and VLOs, accounts for only a minor portion of the total FUV luminosity observed in the dark cloud. Additionally, a comparison between the star formation history of the Milky Way's disk as observed in FUV and near-infrared reveals that the Taurus-Aurigage region is currently experiencing a reduced rate of star formation, about an order of magnitude lower than the average value for the Milky Way's disk. This suggests that the Taurus-Aurigae cloud is one of the few regions where the star formation history as observed in FUV has been found to be consistent with that in near-infrared. Finally, a correlation has been identified between FUV luminosity and H-alpha luminosity observed in the Taurus-Aurigae sources, including VLOs and YSOs. This FUV-H-alpha luminosity ratio is found to be in agreement with the value previously reported for the Orion molecular cloud, indicating that the FUV emission observed in the Taurus-Aurigae sources is primarily a result of radiation from the stars themselves, as opposed to being a consequence of photoionization from the interstellar medium. This implies that the FUV spectral energy distributions of the Taurus-Aurigae sources, including VLOs, are similar to those of the Orion sources, both in shape and total luminosity. Consequently, the use of FUV data for the Taurus-Aurigae sources, including VLOs, is expected to be equivalent to that of the Orion sources, including VLOs, in determining their masses, ages, and star formation efficiencies. Furthermore, the FUV data for the Taurus-Aurigae sources, including VLOs, are expected to be useful in identifying those that are truly embedded, as opposed to being only dust obscured. This is because FUV data are more sensitive to the embedded sources than near-infrared data

To address this gap, we propose five new, streamlined designs that minimize incorrect positive results for specific parameter combinations, while outperforming existing structures in certain scenarios. Specifically, we introduce variations of filter structures incorporating tagged elements, null elements, and special values, as well as null elements paired with filter structures and hash tables designed to capture certain subsets of parameters. Each of these designs offers improved performance and efficiency, and can be used independently or in combination to further reduce incorrect positive results for a broader range of parameters. Our proposals demonstrate that easy-to-implement solutions can achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art results, but with significantly reduced complexity. As such, we expect these designs to serve as attractive alternatives in a wide range of applications. Furthermore, we anticipate that future progress in this area will primarily occur through the development of new algorithms for constructing approximate data structures, rather than relying on more complex and expensive approaches. In this study, we revisit the core features of two regression models that incorporate Bayesian hierarchical structures and control for additional variables. These models, which also have counterparts in frequentist form, are the second-order ordinary differential equation-based mixed model (OEDMm) and the Gaussian process-based regression model (GPR). Our primary objective is to investigate how accurately these models can fit and forecast educational data while accounting for varying rates of growth. We achieve this by simulating data that mirrors the growth trajectory of a subset of students from the PRODYN project and evaluating the performance of OEDMm, GP-R, and their mixed model counterparts on synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, this research aims to identify the advantages and disadvantages of each model type and assess their practical usability. Our findings indicate that the Bayesian OEDMm and GP-R models exhibit notable similarities in frequentist form, which also share similarities in mixed model form. Based on our analyses using synthetic and real data, the OEDMm, GP-R, and their mixed model counterparts demonstrate comparable performance in fitting and predictive tasks, although some models are more effective at forecasting short-term and long-term growth. Notably, the OEDMm and GP-R models are more practical from a computational and theoretical standpoint. Our research also demonstrates the potential of the OEDMm and GP-R models to accurately fit and forecast the growth trajectories of small student groups, and to estimate the effects of additional variables on these trajectories through simulations. Overall, this study highlights the utility of the OEDMm, GP-R, and their mixed model counterparts as useful tools for data and functional regression analysis, and particularly for analyzing the growth rates of small student groups while controlling for additional variables. Our supplementary materials include the R code used to replicate our analyses and provide additional resources. We offer a mathematical expression to determine the winning chances for both the mafia and town factions in the game Mafia/Werewolf.
Our approach is centered on a specific principle: the town's chances of winning are directly tied to the ratio of town to mafia members, while the mafia's chances are inversely related to this ratio.
Assuming the town makes ideal decisions in eliminating players, we analyze how the size of the party and the elimination process influence the town's effectiveness and derive a mathematical formula for the town's winning probability as a function of the number of mafia members and the total number of players.
In particular, when the number of mafia members exceeds 2, the town's winning chances are directly proportional to the 2nd power of the town's advantage over mafia members, and this result is subject to correction terms that diminish at a rate of 1/n, where n represents the total number of players.
Furthermore, when the number of mafia members does not exceed 2, the town's winning chances are directly proportional to the town's advantage over mafia members, and this result is subject to correction terms that diminish at a rate of 1/n, while an additional term of 1/n^2 appears for p=2, and this is verified by comparison with existing numerical estimates for p=3.
Our mathematical expression for the town's winning chances can be employed in two ways: firstly, to derive a lower limit for the town's winning chances as a function of the number of mafia members; secondly, to derive a mathematical expression for the specific winning chances of both factions in the game Mafia/Werewolf when the number of mafia members is 3, and this can be used in conjunction with existing numerical estimates for p=4 to provide an accurate comparison of town and mafia winning chances at a resolution of 1%.
Our approach is unique as it is grounded in the town's elimination processes, whereas previous studies have focused on the mafia's strategies. Our study is particularly notable for its derivation of accurate winning chances at a resolution of 1%, and this is achieved without requiring additional computational tools beyond those available in the game itself. Our mathematical expression for the town's winning chances is universally applicable and can be employed in other games with similar winning conditions to the mafia faction. Our study is a pioneering example of a study that provides winning chances at a resolution of 1%, and this is achieved solely through analytical means, making it a significant advancement in the field. study uses long-term computer simulations of planetary growth from a shared gas
disk, and the results reveal a link between the planets' relative sizes and the

reference time gap is introduced, separating the planets' development, the

planets' mass ratio is most likely to increase as the gas disk supplies them with
material, and the way the planets interact with each other with increasing distance

planets develop in tandem in planetary systems with multiple giant planets. Our
study provides a new perspective on the long-standing debate about planetary
formation theories and offers a novel approach to understanding the coexistence of
giant planets in planetary systems across a range of masses and separations.

models based on observations of planetary systems with multiple giant planets.

While quantum gravity is expected to have no global symmetries, several global symmetries are present in popular effective field theories including the Standard Model and many Cosmology models. Although generally expected that quantum gravity will destroy any global symmetry, many theories have one, and it's often ignored in favor of simpler, symmetric versions.  Global symmetries can be viewed as being akin to crystals, with crystal lattices providing examples of highly ordered systems.  This discussion will explore global symmetries in the context of Particle Physics and Cosmology, focusing on how they are implemented in field theory languages, how known symmetries are represented in the Standard Model and similar frameworks, and how global symmetries are related to other forms of symmetry.  We will also examine potential sources of symmetry breaking, including gravity and stochastic electroweak symmetry breaking.  Finally, we will discuss an alternative approach to global symmetry breaking that may offer a more robust solution to the naturalness problem, along with its implications for Cosmology, particularly on inflation and the Cosmology of the Standard Model.  We conclude with a brief overview of possible experimental signatures of global symmetry breaking.  This discussion is based on a chapter from the Particle Data Review series and incorporates concepts from relevant literature.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were combined with existing optical data, revealing a FUV-to-FUV color-magnitude diagram that suggests a FUV bright FV star within the cluster. Additionally, a FUV color map and surface brightness radial profile of NGC 4147 were constructed, showing the cluster's FUV brightness increases towards the center. Analysis of FUV-to-FUV color-magnitude diagrams and FUV color maps identified no evidence of diffuse gas within the cluster. Further analysis of FV stars' behavior in NGC 4147 revealed a relationship with blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars, suggesting these FV stars might be a subset of BHB stars. Our detection of a FUV bright BHB star, accompanied by the identification of a FV star possibly at the cluster's edge, provides insight into the UV-bright blue straggler star (BSS) population. Our results suggest a FV+BHB to BSS ratio of approximately 1:1, potentially indicating that UV-bright BSSs share a similar evolution path to FV+BHB stars. Our study also identified a FUV bright hot white dwarf (WWDF) candidate within the field of view, with a potential distance of 8.4 kpc based on parallax measurement. Our findings further indicate that the observed hot WWDF has a mass of approximately 0.18 solar masses. The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, researchers continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning. However, malicious actors adapt to these systems by developing evasion attacks that alter their behavior in detected areas. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks, which directly modify the Android malware samples used to train a malware detection model. We propose a novel approach, the Generative Adversarial Problem-space Evasion Attack (GAPA), which utilizes generative adversarial networks to create Android malware samples similar to those in a training dataset, and then modifies these samples to evade detection by altering their feature space. We evaluated GAPA against existing evasion attacks of a similar purpose and a type-based evasion attack that modified Android app features, under the same experimental settings. The results show that GAPA successfully created undetected evasion attacks that effectively demonstrated the vulnerability of state-of-the-art malware detection systems to problem-space evasion attacks. For the purpose of sharing our research, we publicly released our GAPA implementation on a platform that supports collaborative research. Furthermore, our study highlighted the significant impact of problem-space evasion attacks on malware detection systems and recommended the use of robust validation metrics, such as ROC-AUC, to accurately measure an model's performance in detecting evasion attacks. Moreover, our study suggested the implementation of a detection mechanism capable of identifying problem-space evasion attacks and advised researchers to investigate the applicability of few-shot learning in this area. The study concluded by pointing out the need for further investigation into the impact of problem-space evasion attacks on Android malware detection systems. Furthermore, we have established that the Nash equilibrium has a limited number of pricing options, and we have also identified a lower and upper bound for the optimal two-part tariff. We have verified the relevance of our findings through numerical simulations using real-world data from New York City. Our research shows that balancing pooling rates and detours leads to a trade-off, and that by charging more, the provider may actually attract fewer riders. This discovery could have a significant impact on the pricing strategy if confirmed in real-world applications, thereby enabling ridepooling providers to set lower caps, potentially increasing demand and improving service quality while maintaining revenue. Additionally, our study highlights the trade-off between pooling rates and detours through a ridepooling provider's optimal fare, and suggests that a publicly available fare standard could be beneficial to the industry. A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers significant potential for further investigation. At its core, DIM utilizes variational auto-encoders (VAEs) to define a latent space representation of brain data. The model's ability to capture natural patterns in brain scans is enhanced through a contrastive learning mechanism that encourages the extraction of meaningful, spontaneously produced features. In this research, we delve into the specifics of DIM and evaluate its effectiveness by applying it to a specific task: identifying Alzheimer's disease in T1-weighted MRI images. Our implementation of DIM surpasses existing benchmarks, underscoring its potential as a versatile platform for unsupervised learning in brain imaging. Furthermore, we identify key characteristics that contribute to the model's performance and demonstrate how it efficiently detects Alzheimer's disease. Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, where sentences or paragraphs are categorized based on their content. To enhance our comprehension of the text classification models' decision-making processes, it is necessary to attribute the classification outcome to specific word features. Several word-level attribution methods have been proposed to address this requirement. The application of influence scores, which analyze how individual words affect model predictions, has been significant in recent studies. The scores are typically calculated by presenting modified text instances to a model and measuring the resultant changes in predictions and attention distributions. However, determining the optimal data points to use can be challenging in the context of pre-trained language models, which are typically utilized in text classification tasks. The existing methods either employ random selection or fix query data, while disregarding the unique characteristics of text data. In this research, we present an efficient method to manually select significant data points for query construction in the context of text classification, utilizing the variance of word influence scores as a criterion. The proposed data points are subsequently utilized to compute word influence scores through the FaIR framework, which is specifically designed for pre-trained language models. The results demonstrate that the obtained scores are consistent with established methods in word-level attribution and can effectively capture the contributions of rare words. A key advantage of using counterdiabatic protocols in quantum state manipulation lies in their ability to carry out adiabatic processes without the need to slowly change parameters. However, currently available methods mainly focus on systems governed by classical Hamiltonians, making it essential to explore counterdiabatic methods for quantum systems with operator-valued Hamiltonians. We introduce a method for deriving and analyzing (operator-valued) counterdiabatic terms within the Hilbert-Schmidt class, along with developing a criterion for their existence. By utilizing these developments, we're able to derive effective, time-dependent Hamiltonians for arbitrary, unitary transformations between two quantum states. We're also able to demonstrate the existence of counterdiabatic methods for certain classes of operator-valued Hamiltonians, such as linear or quadratic ones, and evaluate their limitations by comparing them against classical Hamiltonians. Finally, we compare the effectiveness of different counterdiabatic methods in facilitating target unitary transformations between two quantum states. Our work lays a solid mathematical foundation for counterdiabatic methods in quantum operator systems. Additionally, our explorations reveal the complexities involved in using counterdiabatic methods for operator-valuid methods, underlining the significance of carefully assessing their existence, limitations, and performance in specific applications. Ultimately, we derive a general principle for achieving adiabatic or counterdiabatic control over arbitrary quantum systems through the combined application of multiple harmonic driving fields. The conditions required for this principle are established in terms of the relative phases and ratios of driving frequencies, making it a universal and flexible method for accomplishing target unitary transformations between two quantum states with high accuracy. Furthermore, we're able to show that this principle can be applied to various types of quantum systems, such as driven two-level systems, free fermions, or any other type of quantum system, as long as they meet the established conditions. The experiments described in this work successfully demonstrate the universal applicability of this principle to different types of driven two-transverse photonic systems. The conditions required for this principle are accurately verified through the experiments, along with the relative phases and frequency ratios of driving fields. The experiments performed successfully demonstrate the unique characteristics of counterdiabatic methods in operator-valued systems, making this method a versatile tool for accomplishing target unitary transformations between two quantum states with high accuracy and self-suppression. We investigate the RDF data exchange problem, where source data with integrity constraints is translated into RDF instances using a target schema. Our study focuses on an RDF formalism that allows typed IRI construction and includes built-in functions, as specified in RDF 1.1 and RDFS, as well. We introduce two new integrity constraints, subject-to-subject and subject-to-object equivalence, in addition to existing tree-like structural constraints. For non-equivalent targets, we develop a algorithmic method to determine a unique RDF instance through data exchange. Furthermore, we establish the feasibility of computing optimal RDF instances when targets have equivalent structures. Our study also explores the complexity of computing optimal RDF instances according to various existing frameworks. Our results show that an optimal RDF instance can be computed in polynomial time for targets with equivalent structures, but this may not be true for other target types. Our study also reveals the high complexity of computing an optimal RDF instance, even under relaxed constraints, when targets are schema-rich. In contrast, we find that determining the existence of a schema-compliant RDF instance is a relatively straightforward problem under certain constraints. Our study lays the groundwork for future research on typed IRI constructors and integrated function applications in RDF data exchange. Our proposed approach is innovative in that it diverges from traditional RDF data exchange methods, which typically rely on adding type annotations to IRIs, in favor of incorporating IRI constructors and built-in functions in a more integrated manner. Our study is also unique in its use of subject-to-subject and subject-to-object equivalence constraints, which are distinct from existing structural integrity constraints in RDF data exchange. Our results are applicable to a variety of real-world scenarios, including data exchange involving identifiers with global meaning, such as user IDs or ISBN book numbers. Our proposed approach is also transferable to other areas of semantic data exchange, such as computing optimal instances of property graphs, which extend the RDF formalism with directed relationships. Our study is further enhanced by the inclusion of additional applications, such as global identifier constraints, prefix-based equivalence, and path-based equivalence, which are all high complexity problems even under relaxed constraints. A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics, operations research and artificial intelligence. Recent advancements in the analysis of productivity and efficiency require sophisticated regression techniques. This paper will review recent developments in shape constrained nonparametric regression and efficient analysis of similar fields. Additionally, the paper will introduce a novel class of artificial neural networks tailored to monotone and unimodal regression functions with a focus on their mathematical underpinnings, generalization capabilities, and demonstrate their effectiveness using real-world data sets, particularly those related to measuring productivity and efficiency. Experimental results show that the proposed monotone and unimodal ANNs achieve superior performance compared to standard deep learning methods and traditional programming languages in both monotone and unimodal regression tasks. Furthermore, the paper will present applications of monotone ANNs in measuring components of labor productivity and assess the energy efficiency of European cities using UNIPEC data. These case studies highlight the potential of monotone ANNs in analyzing production functions and evaluating unimodular performance of univariate services. The source code of the proposed algorithm has been made publicly available. Monotone and unimodal ANNs can be readily accessed through publicly available repositories like https://github.com/timofeygulshin/Monotone-ANNS or https://github.com/timofeygul/UBANNS. Future research directions will also be outlined in this paper. One such promising direction is the development of multivariate monotone and unimodal ANNs using theoretical and numerical methods. This paper aims to inspire future research in the emerging field of deep shape constrained learning. This study presents an innovative mass reconstruction approach for detecting scalar bosons with low masses at the LHC in the processes $pp\to Zh$ and $pp\cos\cos\cos$. By employing a kinematic analysis on the $Z\cos$ system, where $\cos$ represents either a Higgs or other standard model cosinusine boson, the authors demonstrate that the method can yield a mass resolution improvement of approximately two times in the case of the $Z\cos\cos$ channel and one and a half times in the case of the $Z\cos\cos\cos$ channel, without relying on Monte Carlo simulation results. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced sensitivity against systematic uncertainties, as its outcome is directly linked to the mass value. The method also features a straightforward physics interpretation, where the mass value corresponds to the peak of a probability distribution constructed from the momenta of the leptons in the $Z\cos$ system. This approach can be applied to the observation and measurement of the Higgs boson in the context of the Higgs boson's decays into invisible particles at the LHC, as well as in the detection of light bosons resulting from the decays of the Higgs boson or other particles. Moreover, the authors investigate the feasibility of the proposed method in the presence of background events, such as top quark pair production in association with a Higgs boson or other standard model cosinusine bosons. They show through simulation results that the method can distinguish the signal from background events with a probability greater than 90\%. This approach can also be employed at future colliders operating at centre-of-mass energies of up to 100 TeV. Furthermore, the authors investigate the method's potential for observing particles with masses as light as 10 GeV, while assuming that the detection efficiency remains constant. They find that the method can provide a discovery significance of approximately 10$\sigma$ for particles with masses up to 20 GeV in the case of the $Z\cos\cos$ channel and up to 30 GeV in the case of the $Z\cos\cos\cos$ channel. This approach can also be used to explore beyond the standard model scenarios involving cosinusine bosons with masses ranging from a few GeV to tens of GeV, such as the lightest supersymmetric neutralinos $\tilde{\chi}_1^0$ and $\tilde{\chi}_1^\pm$. Pre-trained language models have revolutionized the field of natural language processing by providing effective representations for numerous NLP tasks. Notably, the Transformer's multi-head attention mechanism plays a pivotal role in learning semantic relationships between words. This paper investigates the impact of word syntactic relationships on self-attention and proposes a novel method to integrate syntactic parsing into the Transformer for enhanced performance in a downstream task, part-of-speech tagging. We employ two linear projection matrices, one for queries and one for keys, within the self-attention mechanism, drawing on the syntax from a pre-trained parser as pseudo-syntax for the words. We then subject the model to syntactic constraints during training. Our experimental findings demonstrate that this approach successfully captures syntactic information and improves the model's accuracy in the absence of additional syntax-related supervision or parallel data. We further analyze the efficacy of the multi-head attention mechanism by examining the impact of each head on the model's performance and identify the head primarily influenced by syntax, specifically the second head (head 1). Ultimately, our proposed method yields superior results, with an average improvement in test set accuracy of around 1.3 percentage points compared to the baseline model. We also observe that the model's performance peaks at about 1.1 points above the baseline when using four heads, specifically heads 7 and 8, which are most sensitive to syntax. We discuss the model's improved performance in the context of syntax-based attention. The code developed for this research is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/brunovieira95/syn-self-attention. Our paper contributes to the understanding of the self-attention mechanism by highlighting its capacity to model word syntactic relationships, specifically in pre-trained models, and demonstrates its potential to be a general-purpose syntax module. Furthermore, our proposed method offers a practical solution to integrate syntax into the Transformer's architecture without requiring additional training or parallel data, thus facilitating the development of more effective and transparent models for NLP tasks. The potential for generalizing the approach to other tasks, such as machine comprehension, is also explored. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the self-attention mechanism can effectively model syntax, pointing to a promising future for large language models as general-purpose syntax modules. The novel application of self-attention to syntax analysis may lead to a new understanding of the mechanism and its potential to learn from syntax, potentially rivaling performance with properly fine-tuned models in the future. The final model's source code is available at https://github.com/brunovieira95

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data in certain languages hinders their full potential realization. This study aims to improve the accuracy of German ASR models by supplementing existing Kaldi models with a larger dataset of spoken information. The chosen dataset comprises Wikipedia content read by volunteers, which significantly expands the available data but requires cleaning to ensure quality. After processing the data, we evaluate the effectiveness of the enhanced models and observe notable improvements, with the top-performing model achieving a relative improvement of 8.8% in terms of word error rate on the Tuda-SD corpus. Notably, this improvement is largely due to the models' ability to recognize out-of-vocabulary words, which would otherwise remain unrecognizable. ASR models based on this Wikipedia data also demonstrate impressive robustness, with the top model experiencing only a 1.2% decline in performance in the presence of background noise and exhibiting a 3.4% decrease in the presence of a second speaker, into a 5dB signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, the integration of this data into multilingual acoustic models yields a relative improvement of 7.1% in the Tuda-SD corpus and a 6.3% improvement in the Tuda-VD corpus. Notably, the enhanced models based on multilingual acoustic models show less decline in performance in the presence of noise and a second speaker, with a 3.1% difference in the Tuda-SD corpus and a 2.3% difference in the Tuda-VD corpus. The outcome of this study indicates that the spoken Wikipedia corpus constitutes a valuable resource for enhancing the accuracy and robustness of German ASR models, with the potential to produce high-quality ASR output even in the presence of background noise and overlapping speech. The findings of this research are expected to contribute to the development of high-performance ASR models for other low-resourced languages, given that Wikipedia is a widely available source of information across the globe. The proposed methodology is versatile and can be easily replicated in other languages, which in turn may yield better results in ASR tasks. Ultimately, the use of Wikipedia data is expected to yield better outcomes in speech-based applications, thereby reducing reliance on manual transcription and accelerating the development of speech-based technologies. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas, such as the medical field. Previous research has attempted to address this by developing methods to reveal the underlying features that a model extracts. Nevertheless, existing approaches either rely on modifications to the model architecture or require additional processing of the model outputs, which is not always feasible. Furthermore, these methods primarily focus on the final layer's representations, neglecting earlier layers. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications, (ii) limited precision of 8-bit fixed-point arithmetic, and (iii) a streamlined structure with fewer parameters and a compact layout. We compare the performance of CNN and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks on platforms like Raspberry Pi, and we evaluate existing NN architectures for keyword spotting in terms of accuracy, processing speed, and energy efficiency on platforms like ARM Cortex-M7 MCUs and Raspberry Pi. Our Compact CNN achieves high accuracy (97.5%) and efficient processing/energy usage, outperforming NNs and surpassing current state-of-the-art keyword spotting methods. The source code for the Compact CNN is publicly available at https://github.com/ashishgupta99/Compact-CNN-Keyword-Spotting. To this end, we develop a framework where an internal controller uses an enhanced simulator that includes an additional component to counter adversarial influence, while the simulator is trained using a variational approach. Our findings demonstrate that this algorithm is nearly optimal even when the adversary exercises full control over the environment. Our approach is evaluated using the benchmark benchmark of linear quadratic regulation. Investigating the quantum particle tunneling process requires careful consideration 
in order to differentiate true tunneling from detection delays due to phase shift 
accumulation during the classically forbidden region traversal. A commonly used 
tunneling time metric, the Larmor precession time, is problematic as it doesn't 
distinguish particle position and can't distinguish the front or the tail of the tunneling wavepacket. We propose an alternative approach that utilizes the tunneling 
wavepacket's peak position to calculate tunneling time, effectively disregarding 
Larmor precession time measurements. By applying this new metric to several 
well-studied systems, we demonstrate that it mirrors previously established 
tunneling time results, thus providing a clear distinction between tunneling and 
detector-related time delays. Furthermore, this approach enables determination of 
tunneling times for wavepactch components other than the peak, offering fresh 
insights into the tunneling process. It's worth noting that this method relies on 
precise wavepacket knowledge, which isn't typically available in experimental 
settings. Nonetheless, this issue could be resolved with improved wavepacket 
reconstruction techniques. Moreover, we show that tunneling times measured using 
the tunneling window method are equivalent to those obtained with the peak 
detecting method. Consequently, this validates the tunneling window approach as 
a correct way to distinguish true tunneling times from detection delays. A final 
thought is presented where the proposed detecting method is adapted to potential 
tunneling scenarios, thus providing a new perspective on tunneling time 
determination. Potential tunneling refers to situations where tunneling times 
appear to be negative, often resulting from the tunneling wavepacket entering the 
classically forbidden region or the detector being out of the tunneling region. 
In such cases, tunneling times can be determined by employing the proposed peak 
detecting method, thus offering a new perspective on tunneling time 
determination. Potential tunneling is an interesting phenomenon that has been 
previously explored in several studies, and a brief overview of its analysis is 
presented. Moreover, a new analysis of potential tunneling is presented, focusing 
on situations where tunneling times are negative, thus providing a new 
understanding of tunneling times and their behavior. A recent discussion on

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra that remains unconstrained by the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining whether this algebra is at least a Poisson algebra capable of being promoted to a quantum algebra has remained unresolved. We tackle this question by first establishing the commutator of asymptotic symmetries on Minkowski space and then extending our findings to gravity. We demonstrate that the extended BMS algebra is indeed a Hopf algebra with a well-defined coproduct, but the commutator of asymptotic symmetries in null infinity does not extend to gravity. Specifically, in null infinity, the commutator of superdipole charges is rendered finite due to the absence of a physical phase, whereas in gravity, the corresponding superdipole operator is found to be nonzero, thereby casting doubt on the notion that the extended BMS algebra can be promoted to a quantum algebra. We observe that this is a universal shortcoming affecting all null symmetries, including new asymptotic symtries introduced recently. We further explore whether this shortcoming persists when a physical phase is reintroduced and assess the relevance of this finding to the quantum gravity S-matrix. We reveal that while the extended BMS algebra may be a quantum algebra when a physical phase is absent, such a promotion is not possible when a physical phase is present. We establish that the quantum gravity S-matrix is invariant under the action of the extended BMS algebra, but this invariance is not sufficient to impose a physical phase using the quantum master equation. We observe that this shortcoming persists when considering a larger class of asymptotic symmetries, including the new ones. This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models encompassing both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. We calculate the upper and lower bounds on the optimal strategic payoff for both players in this game, its two-player payoff being the sum of individual payoffs from separate games. Moreover, the bounds on payoffs for the insurer and the capitalist are derived for a specific game scenario known as the Black-Scholes game. This work relies on the Lamperti transformation and involves complex calculations to derive approximate expressions for the optimal payoffs in terms of the model parameters, with these estimates proving to be precise in the case of the Black-Scholes game when one of the players adopts an optimal strategy. To approximate the payoff functions, the infinite boundary limits of certain functions and integrals are calculated, allowing for the derivation of precise approximations for specific scenarios. Numerical illustrations demonstrate how the proposed approximation technique can be used to solve the given games numerically. This work further generalizes prior research, such as that found in Cheng et al. (2021), by considering a broader category of games. Specifically, the upper bounds derived in this work are more precise and approach asymptotic optimality under certain conditions, whereas the lower bounds are exact and do not involve asymptotes. Finally, the paper suggests potential research directions for improving the accuracy of the approximations derived. These involve calculating the optimal strategies for the players and the boundary limits of certain functions and integrals, both of which are crucial components in understanding the approximate payoff functions, as well as deriving exact solutions for specific game scenarios. Key findings from this research include the following: (1) the approximate payoff functions provide a precise generalization of the Black-Scholes game; (2) the boundary limits of certain functions and integrals play a crucial role in approximating the optimal payoffs; and (3) the accuracy of the approximations can be enhanced by increasing the number of discrete time increments in the original differential equation. This work ultimately aims to provide a novel approximation technique for a broad category of stochastic differential investment and reinsurance games, as well as deriving exact solutions for specific game scenarios, both of which are crucial components in understanding the underlying reinsurance models. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. Its tracking system, based in the barrel section, relies on the silicon pixel detector (SPD) for initial particle detection. Following the conclusion of Run 2 in 2018, the SPD underwent maintenance, upgrading, and refurbishment in preparation for the challenging conditions of the High-Luminosity (HL-LHC) phase, expected to begin in 2026. Focusing on the HL-LHC's increased radiation environment and the resulting long-term degradation of the SPD's front-end readout electronics, researchers investigated the progressive deterioration of the SPD's performance and proposed a system for monitoring sensor temperature, in order to maintain optimal operating conditions and effective particle detection. Using the sensor's front-end readout electronics and a temperature-sensing unit, the research team created an electronic management system to monitor and analyze the SPD's performance over time, comparing the results of different sensors and front-end readout systems. Through comprehensive data analysis, the researchers identified several key parameters that characterize the SPD's operating behavior and assessed its ability to maintain acceptable levels of performance under the HL-LHC's expected conditions. Furthermore, integrating graphics processing units (GPUs) significantly accelerated the analysis of the SPD's front-end readout data, enabling real-time monitoring and prediction of the detector's long-term behavior and its response to transient radiation events. Overall, the research demonstrated the feasibility and benefits of real-time monitoring and analysis of the SPD's performance, paving the way for the SPD's operation during the HL-LHC phase and the successful detection of high-energy collisions. Moreover, the research showcased the potential of the SPD's front-end readout electronics to operate reliably in extreme radiation environments and the effectiveness of GPU-based acceleration in maintaining control over the SPD's complex digital system. Finally, the research highlighted the value of the SPD's front-end readout electronics in its ability to measure various parameters, including its electrical characteristics under extreme radiation, the SPD's ability to operate in high-energy collisions, and its resilience to long-term degradation and repair under the HL-LHC's increased radiation environment. The research further explored the SPD's ability to maintain its signal integrity and tracking efficiency despite the degradation of its front-end readout electronics and proposed a new monitoring system to ensure the SPD's operation during the HL-LHC phase, based on its performance during Run 2 and in various simulated radiation environments. These nucleon-nucleon interactions, denoted as NN- correlations, primarily occur at short ranges due to the short-lived forces involved. By introducing an energy distribution associated with these correlations, scientists can gain insights into their impact on the nucleus. By analyzing the energy dispersion, researchers can quantify the role of NN-correlations in relation to the overall energy of the nucleus. Studies have demonstrated that NN-correlations account for a significant portion of the nucleus's kinetic energy but have a negligible effect on its total energy. Although NN-correlations do not significantly affect binding energies, their inclusion is essential for achieving agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental data in the scattering analyses. Additionally, NN-correlations' impact on the momentum distribution of the nucleus is observed in proton removal reactions, which shows that their effect is more pronounced at high momenta. Furthermore, by comparing the momentum distribution of the nucleus with and without NN-correlations, researchers can quantify the role of short-range correlations in the nucleus. By comparing the momentum ratio with the binding energy ratio, scientists can distinguish between SRRCs and other influences on the momentum distribution. Our research demonstrates that SRRCs are responsible for a significant portion of the nucleus's momentum around high magnitudes and that separating SRRCs is crucial for accurately analyzing the QCD evolution of the momentum distribution. The separation approach, however, fails to reveal SRRCs at low magnitudes, suggesting that other phenomena, such as the fluctuations from the ground state wave function, are also influential in this region. Consequently, an accurate separation of SRRCs requires accounting for these fluctuations as well. In conclusion, our work highlights the importance of separating SRRCs from other effects in order to understand the role of short-range correlations in the nucleus. We are studying complex scaling as an inherent property unique to complex number systems and its applications. By extending the complex domain without considering complex scaling, we miss an essential aspect, treating complex numbers only as advanced real systems. Our research focuses on developing complex scaling for complex number representations within complex domain learning, particularly in neural networks, which are prevalent in various applications. We compare traditional complex domain learning methods with our new complex learning framework based on complex scaling, at both theoretical and empirical levels. Our results indicate that complex scaling offers better performance in numerous complex learning tasks, supported by analytical evidence and experimental verification. Additionally, our two complex learning methods exhibit distinct characteristics in terms of their objectives, parameter configurations, and complexities, which are analyzed using Taylor expansion and numerical computation. Our findings demonstrate that complex scaling is a valuable computer science concept that can contribute to machine learning, particularly in neural networks, while also expanding its potential applications. Moreover, our proposed complex learning methods based on scaling are straightforward, making them easily adaptable in various scenarios, such as neural networks, signal processing, and computer graphics. Our work is the first to integrate scaling into the complex domain, offering a new understanding and a more efficient approach to complex learning. We hope that our new perspective and methods can bridge the gap between complex number theory and computer science, leading to a better appreciation of complex numbers, which are often considered only as advanced real numbers. A thorough investigation of abundance patterns in 1036 metal-poor stars (<Fe> = 2.0) residing within the Milky Way's disk and halo has been conducted. Using the high-resolution HARPS-NN spectra, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of abundance ratios across 15 key elements from strontium to europium with a median error margin of approximately 0.02 dex. Through a Bayesian analysis, the research evaluated the intrinsic abundance scatter and trends across various elements in the sample population. Results indicate significant intrinsic abundance variability in metal-poor stars with scatter in [X/Fe] abundance ratios ranging from 0.04-0.16 (1σ). Specifically, the study found [Ba/Fe], [Na/Fe], and [Cs/Fe] exhibiting the highest and lowest intrinsic abundance scatter, respectively. Moreover, the research found europium abundance ratios [Eu/Fe] displaying a pronounced decline with decreasing metallicity. Notably, the study discovered a pronounced europium abundance deficit in the Milky Way's early halo, supporting the existence of the r-process nucleosynthesis process. Our findings also suggest that the majority of the europium content in the Milky Way's disk originated from supernovae events associated with core-collapse rather than pair-instability. Additionally, the research found minimal to moderate variations in the abundance ratios of key elements over time within the Milky Way's disk and halo. Our study's results, which are consistent with the majority of previous studies, are well-explained by the galaxy's accretion of dwarf satellites throughout the Milky Way's life. The conventional machine learning framework assumes that the relationships between
variables are consistent across time, but in reality, this is rarely the case.
Consequently, machine learning algorithms often overlook the impact of missing
data, leading to significant biases and inaccuracies. Ignoring unobserved
variables can result in flawed predictions, as highlighted by the example of
Amazon's machine learning-based employment tool being biased against women.
The machine learning community acknowledges the importance of addressing bias and
uncertainty, but current methods are often limited to isolated cases and
cannot be easily adapted to more complex problems. Moreover, there is a shortage
of algorithms capable of modeling complex interactions between multiple variables.
To address these challenges, we propose a novel machine learning algorithm,
Bayescos, designed to tackle high-dimensional problems, including combinatorial
ones, while providing an interpretable model and quantifying uncertainty.

distribution within the context of a cosmological simulation. The performance

computational requirements. The proposed model allows for an in-depth analysis

When we introduce a uniform flow and an activity gradient, the system's collective motion is significantly impacted. While maintaining its overall shape, the dimers exhibit varying behaviors based on the activity gradient. At low gradients, they demonstrate diffusive motion and follow the equation for a force-free particle movement. However, when the gradient exceeds a certain threshold, they begin to move directionally in the direction of the activity's gradient. By employing a mean-field analysis, we are able to derive a Langevin equation that captures the system's dynamic response, and this can be further mapped onto an effective viscosity and osmotic pressure. Notably, our results reveal that active contributions to viscosity and osmotic pressure follow distinct power-law relationships with the activity level, and these relationships can be understood within the context of a linearized Fick's law. Moreover, by introducing uniform flows and activity gradients into such a system, it is found that actin and microtubules can be drawn towards each other under certain conditions, and this can be made to happen in a direction-dependent manner through the adjustment of activity gradients, flow speeds, and disassembly rates. This could potentially be studied using a live cell microscope, and our results suggest that by adjusting parameters appropriately, it is feasible to induce a situation similar to that of active colloid dimers in vivo. Our results also show that active colloids and biopolymers can serve as model systems to explore and understand the behavior of disordered actin filaments and microtubules in living cells, and this in turn may aid in understanding how these filaments are arranged in space within cells. Epidemics can be effectively modeled by mathematics, but a limitation of most models is that they don't account for varying contact rates among different groups within a population. We propose an new method to address this issue, which involves identifying and monitoring changes in these groups over time. By applying this approach to a basic SIR model, we demonstrate that it retains the model's simplicity while enabling the detection of significant population shifts that can impact the model's predictions. We also use this method to re-examine the early spread of COVID-19 in Daegu, South Korea, and show how to use the model to identify key events and estimate the date of detectable cases. Our analysis suggests that COVID-19 began spreading in Daegu about a week before it was officially reported, and that a major population shift occurred in mid-April, about a month before the city's lockdown. Our findings highlight the importance of monitoring and understanding these group dynamics in the early stages of an epidemic. Furthermore, by applying this approach to various populations, it may be possible to identify hidden factors contributing to the success or failure of public health interventions. We introduce Gromov centrality as a general framework unifying multiple network centrality metrics, when normalized. The findings demonstrate that gromov centrality and the triangle inequality exhibit a direct linear relationship. Furthermore, we establish that metrics deviating from linearity by more than 0.1 imply a lack of optimal association with degree or clustering coefficients. Additionally, we show that network centrality metrics also correlate with the exponential mixing time of the Markov chain, although more broadly. This strategy also yields an unbiased distribution for sampling a spanning tree in an graph with a treewidth of O(n^(1−ε)) in a manner that is both consistent and Borel measurable. Specifically, we achieve a treewidth of O(n^(0.39)) for graphs with no K_8-minors (K_8 being the smallest possible value for h). Historically, the treewidth bound improvement here has a long-standing connection to the hosted problem of determining whether a graph has a subgraph consisting of a path whose alternating edge degrees along the path alternate between d and 4 (the d-4-path problem). We then develop AskewSGD, which is the first optimization method capable of addressing all constraints simultaneously. AskewSGD can be seamlessly integrated into existing training frameworks as a scalable and flexible algorithm. Our experiments demonstrate that AskewSGD achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, reducing the number of iterations required to achieve a given accuracy by 43% to 54% on various benchmarks, including ResNet50-CIFAR10, ResNet50-SIMONYAN, VGG16-SIMONYAN, MobileNetV2-CIFAR10, MobileNetV2-SIMONYAN, MobileNetV2-TFSL, Wide-ResNet-40-CIFAR10, and ResNet50-TFSL. In ultracold Bose gases, where non-conservation of energy is prevalent, two-particle correlations exhibit oscillating behavior. The underlying frequencies of these oscillations are linked to the imaginary component of the Liouvillian gap, $\Gamma$. A theoretical model employing the mean-field approximation was used to determine the Liouvillian gap in a one- and two-dimensional Bose gas system. The results show that, in one dimension, the imaginary component of the Liouvillian gap is zero, leading to non-oscillating two-particle correlations in this dimension. For two dimensions, the Liouvillian gap was calculated as a function of the non-thermalization rate $\Gamma_6$, and the resulting behavior is characterized by oscillations whose amplitude decreases over time. A comparison with the mean-field approximation showed that the model accurately predicts two-particle correlation functions, thus validating the mean-field approximation for this system. The model's ability to capture non-conservative behavior in ultracold Bose gases may have implications for their classification as conservative or non-conservative systems. Furthermore, the model's application to higher dimensions could provide insights into the transition from conservative to non-conservative behavior. The theoretical model developed in this work may also facilitate a more nuanced understanding of the behavior of quantum systems, where non-conservation of energy can lead to complex and dynamic patterns. Such an understanding may have far-reaching applications in the field of quantum simulation. Ultimately, the model's predictions of two-particle correlation functions could be experimentally verified, thereby confirming the model's accuracy and utility. The theoretical model developed in this work could be adapted or modified to analyze other non-conservative quantum systems. Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed.  Specifically, optimizing task success using reinforcement learning alone often leads to low lexical diversity in task-oriented settings, causing generated text to seem unrealistic and made-up.  Moreover, algorithms tend to struggle when dealing with out-of-vocabulary words, failing to learn how to effectively use compound words.  Our proposed solution is Dicta, a paradigm for generating text through explicit memory management.  Dicta employs a separate neural memory network to directly select relevant words and phrases based on a given context, then uses them as targets for a generative model.  By doing so, Dicta addresses the issues mentioned above.  Our experiments in both semantic parsing and question answering dialogue benchmarks confirm that Dicta outperforms current state-of-the-art models in terms of natural language generation, as well as out-of-vocabulary performance.  Additionally, Dicta's ability to learn about compound words is successful, while its explicit memory management also facilitates a better understanding of word semantics.  Our project, including code and data, can be accessed at https://github.com/allenai/Dicta.  A demo of Dicta can be seen at https://dicta.allenai.github.io/.  A pre-trained model similar to the one used in our experiments can be accessed at https://dicta.allenai.github.io/demo/.  A future version of Dicta will be used to support the semantic parsing component of the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence's Refer system, which will be described in a separate paper. Additionally, $R_\infty$ groups inherently possess a robust conjugating structure, which enables the existence of a conjugating function that transcends any automorphism $\varphi$ of G, thereby mapping conjugating pairs $(x_1, x_2)$ to conjugating pairs $(a_1, a_2)$. It is shown that the conjugating function's properties are uniform across all automorphisms and are defined by the group's prime factors. Consequently, we prove that automorphisms in $R_\infty$ groups are strongly conjugating under specific conditions. In particular, for $R_\infty$ groups where the conjugating function's prime $p$ satisfies $[p, 2] = 1$, we show that automorphisms $\varphi$ are strongly conjugating if and only if $\varphi^2$ is also an automorphism. This criterion is illustrated through a key example, which highlights a group G of which the third twist is $R_\infty$ but the second twist is not strongly conjugating. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in over 100 million reported cases and more than 3 million deaths worldwide, prompting the rapid development and deployment of contact tracing applications to assist in containing the outbreak. These apps, however, have raised significant privacy concerns as they often monitor users' movements, thereby posing a risk to their anonymity. The implementation of Traceable yet Untraceable Transactions (TUT) in Bitcoin has been an effective measure in preventing adversary-controlled entities from deanonymizing users, by employing a combination of mixing pools and coin join techniques. Drawing inspiration from this concept, we propose a decentralized, self-sustaining framework for the development of privacy-preserving contact tracing apps, by merging local transmission records with a cryptocurrency like Bitcoin through the application of TUT. By utilizing a secure multi-party computation protocol, we show that the aggregated metadata from a predefined number of users can be securely transferred to authorities, while maintaining the anonymity of each user, however, at a certain cost to location precision. The feasibility of this framework has been verified through simulation experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in preventing single-user attacks, while significantly reducing the effective entropy in double-user attacks. The resulting contact tracing apps demonstrate a notable trade-off between location precision and user anonymity. The experimental results show an optimal balance between location precision and user anonymity can be achieved with a suitable configuration of the number of users and the number of batches in TUT. The framework, however, fails to provide any location information when the number of users is high, the number of batches is large, and the transmission probability is low. The source code of this framework is available at \url{https://github.com/zhousl/COVID19ContactTracing}. The research presented in this paper has been supported by NSF Grant No. 1950810. The central notion of quantum entanglement revolves around the idea that it generates measurable interactions between particles that have been entangled. Nonetheless, entanglement itself doesn't predict the extent or magnitude of the correlation. Additionally, entanglement can't be used to transmit information about one particle to another. Exploring the implications of this concept, a quantum protocol has been devised which demonstrates the following: entanglement of two particles indeed ensures the existence of measurable interactions, but only in the context of a specific distribution of outcomes when measurements are taken in specific states. Surprisingly, this same distribution of outcomes holds no significance in describing the outcome distribution of a different entanglement measure - the relative entropy of entanglement. In fact, the relative entropy of entanglement fails to capture the measurable interactions generated by entanglement. Consequently, the entanglement measure known as the quantum discord is required to describe the measurable interactions generated by entanglement. Notably, however, the quantum discord also falls short of predicting the extent or magnitude of the interaction in this context. The situation becomes even more intriguing as it has also been shown that entanglement with a specific form - the GHZ type - generates measurable interactions but only when measurements are taken in certain states. Once again, the relative entropy of entanglement fails to capture the measurable interactions generated by GHZ entanglement, but this time the quantum discord is sufficient to predict the extent or magnitude of the interaction generated by GHZ entanglement. The findings presented here underscore the significance of choosing an appropriate measure of entanglement that aligns with the specific phenomenon being studied. Furthermore, the results illustrate how different measures of entanglement can provide unique insights into distinct aspects of entanglement. Finally, the results demonstrate how entanglement protocols can serve as valuable tools for shedding light on fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. The specific protocol developed here is based on an entanglement-assisted communication scenario - the entanglement-assisted communication with two parties - and involves a simple communication scenario where two parties share two copies of an entangled state. When measurements are taken in specific states, the protocol generates correlations that can be described by measures of entanglement. However, when measurements are taken in other states, the protocol generates correlations that can be described by quantum discord. The specific protocol developed here is an extension of a previously proposed protocol that utilized a different measure of entanglement known as the squashed entanglement.
