A statistical analysis of 42 protostellar cores, 26 starless cores, and 25 massive starless cores within 11.0 km/s of the Ori A molecular cloud was conducted by comparing their submillimeter luminosities and far-infrared-ratio methods. Protostellar and starless cores within this cloud were selected based on their submillimeter luminosities and far-infrared-ratio values, with the aim of comparing their mass-to-line intensity ratios. A notable distinction between the mass distribution of protostellar and starless cores was observed, with the former possessing significantly more mass when using the far-infrared-ratio method than the far-infrared method. Conversely, no substantial discrepancy in mass was found when using the far-infrared-ratio method for the selected starless cores. Our data suggest that high mass values measured from the far-infrared-ratio method of protostellar cores are likely due to the emission of warm dust caused by the outflows of young stars. Furthermore, a comparison of our results with previous studies indicates that high mass values measured from the far-infrared-ratio method of massive cores are likely due to the emission of warm dust caused by radiation pressure feedback from nearby massive young stars. Our data also suggest that a significant portion of massive cores within the cloud could be proto-clumps affected by this process. Finally, a correlation between the outflow signifiers and mass values measured from the far-infrared-ratio method for protostellar cores was observed, with the aid of radiative transfer modeling revealing that the outflow signifiers are primarily influenced by the outflow luminosity rather than the outflow mass or the IR luminosity. Our data suggest that warm dust emission significantly contributes to the mass values measured from the far-infrared-ratio method for protostellar and starless cores within the cloud. Therefore, we propose the implementation of a dust emission correction factor to mass values measured from this method to reduce bias. Our results also highlight the importance of considering the influence of outflow emission when using outflow signifiers to diagnose protostellar activity. Fortunately, Bayesian deep learning offers a way to characterize uncertainty by treating model weights as random variables. Research has demonstrated that this approach can differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic uncertainty. In this study, we revisit key principles in Bayesian deep learning, focusing on the recognition that intrinsic uncertainty can often be mitigated by accessing additional data. We also revisit the application of Gaussian processes in unsupervised learning and control problems, particularly in systems with complex dynamics. We then explore the challenges of scaling Bayesian deep learning to complex models, including large datasets and high-dimensional images. Finally, we discuss future avenues for research, including the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic uncertainty. This research is based on notes from a tutorial presented at the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning. The full tutorial, titled "Bayesian Deep Learning: Advances in learning uncertainty over complex hierarchical models for autonomous systems," is available online. We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,T(-1),B,X) in the left half-plane for a closed and densely defined operator B with domain B+. Consequently, this relationship affects the stability of a non-homogeneous linear system governed by the equation ξ'(t) = Bξ(t) + a(t), where ξ(0) = ξ0 in X. Our findings offer an alternative to existing theorems that typically require the boundedness of the resolvent over the right half-plane. We also establish that solutions of a Lyapunov inequality in L1(0,T,X) provide sufficient conditions for the exponential stability of the homogeneous system ξ'(t) = Bξ(t), where ξ(0) = ξ0 in X. The specific examples of the operator B and initial value ξ0 further illustrate these findings. Our study draws inspiration from previous work, particularly those of Hu in 2019 and Zelazo in 2020. We investigate the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a variety of bosonic environments. Our research reveals that the quality of these quasiparticles relies substantially on the interaction between the fermions and a broader set of bosonic excitations that are specifically tuned to a resonant frequency. The instability of the quasiparticles manifests itself through a progressive loss of momentum upon each interaction. Consequently, the quasiparticles exhibit a tendency towards momentum-conserving decay into bosonic excitations when their dispersion relation features a flat section. This phenomenon can potentially be observed in a range of systems, such as cold atoms, the unitary Fermi gas, doped graphene, and doped semiconductor materials in the presence of photonic excitations. Furthermore, the phenomenon of quasiparticle instability due to a bosonic environment may also explain the experimentally observed decrease in phase space asymmetry in the unitary Fermi gas under the influence of two-photon Raman spectroscopy. Similarly, the phenomenon of quasiparticle instability may also account for the experimentally observed underestimation of phase space asymmetry in the unitary Fermi gas as measured via three-photon Raman spectroscopy. Our research also extends to the study of quasiparticles in the presence of a bosonic environment that is detuned from resonance. Our results reveal that the quasiparticles are stable in this case and exhibit characteristics resembling those of soliton quasiparticles. Our research provides a range of potential experimental tests to verify the phenomenon of quasiparticle instability in a variety of systems, such as the observation of quasiparticle momentum dissipation via Raman spectroscopy, photoemission, and the detection of quasiparticle soliton formation using three-photon Raman spectroscopy. This paper introduces a new class of orthogonal polynomials related to Jacobi polynomials with logarithmic weights, and we explore the asymptotic behavior of the associated Stieltjes transforms. Furthermore, we use Riesz projections to link these polynomials to a family of de Branges spaces of entire polynomials, and we confirm the polynomials' orthogonality under the specified weights. Additionally, we outline a method for generating explicit polynomials and provide an initial set of examples. This investigation stems from a similar study of classical orthogonal polynomials with logarithmic weights, which revealed an unexpected connection to Fyodorov, Khoruzhenko, and Sommers' 2003 findings on orthogonal polynomials associated with Ginibre point processes. Similarities and differences between the two scenarios are discussed in the concluding section. de Branges spaces of entire polynomials show considerable promise in the study of integrals involving Toeplitz forms and Hankel matrices, and this work includes a demonstration of how to compute a specific integral related to logarithmic Jacobi polynomials. As a result, we derive a novel expression for a related constant of integration, and we verify a conjecture posed by one of the paper's co-authors stating that this constant remains non-negative for all relevant parameter values. Related to this, we also explore the asymptotic behavior of certain Hankel determinants for logarithmic Jacobi polynomials as the degree of the polynomials tends to infinity, and we confirm a conjecture stating that these determinants evaluate to either zero or a non-complex value. In the process of investigating these determinants, we establish a non-numeric relationship describing their possible values, which may be of independent interest. Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled workers before evaluation tasks are initiated, and subsequently collect reliable annotations while managing recruitment costs. The proposed approach serves as a model for selecting qualified annotators in other complex annotation endeavors. Furthermore, to facilitate efficient summuration of lengthy documents, we introduce a novel hierarchical summarization model, which enables the breakdown of large documents into concise summaries at multiple hierarchical levels, thereby facilitating user selection of an optimal level of summary. The summration system is publicly accessible at https://documentsummarizer.github.io. Figures and other supplementary material are available online at https://documentsummarizer.github.io/supplement. The source code is available at https://github.com/adam-quantum/document-summarization. Speaking of the data collection process, we collect documents from publicly available sources, including arXiv and ResearchGate, whereas crowdsourced annotations are stored in the hierarchical format and distributed through Amazon Mechanical Turk. The model design is inspired by the work of Sotaro Mi, et al., which proposes a hierarchical summarization model, although our work deviates in addressing document complexity, annotator quality, and hierarchical summarization with a hierarchical document structure in mind. Text-video retrieval has emerged as a vital task for understanding the temporal relationship between vision and language, allowing for the identification of relevant video segments that match query texts. A common approach involves embedding both text and vision components into a unified multimodal space, then selecting a optimal segment from available choices. However, current methods often neglect the distinct vocabularies between vision and language, leading to inaccurate alignment and performance limitations. To bridge this gap, our proposed TS2-Net, short for Token Shift Residual Transform, introduces a novel architecture that integrates token shift and residual transform modules. The token shift module reorders vision tokens according to their corresponding language counterparts' importance scores, while the residual transform module adjusts vision and language components through element-wise operations. By doing so, we can effectively minimize vision-language discrepancies and create more accurate cross-modal representations, as demonstrated by the increase in performance over baseline models. Additionally, our proposed TS2-Net achieves state-of-the-art results on popular text-video retrieval benchmarks, including MSRVTT, MSVD, ActivityNet, and VATEX, across various settings. The code and model weights are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/whs1218/TS2-Net. Furthermore, our method also won the first place in MSRVTT and third place in MSVD and ActivityNet from the CVPR2022 workshop, as well as the second place in the ViViT challenge from NeurIPS2022. This degree distribution can be expressed using a power law that has an exponential cutoff, and this behavior has been observed in numerous real-world networks. In response to criticism that combining rules doesn't accurately represent how nodes attach to each other, we have developed a discrete-time framework for preferential identification. In this framework, a new node connects to existing nodes with weights determined by the ratios of their attachment rates to their current degrees. Using both continuous-time and discrete-time frameworks in a backwards approach, we have derived closed-form expressions for the expected degrees of early nodes in both scenarios. These expressions confirm that combining rules lead to a power law distribution with an exponential cutoff. To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary systems, we must rely on accurate quantum mechanics theories. This project involves rectifying the inaccuracies in previous quantum mechanics interpretations, eliminating extraneous calculations and parameters that have complicated the field. We introduce more suitable approaches to understand how gravitational forces affect quantum systems. This work specifically focuses on how gravitational forces impact particles with mass dependent on location, placed within a background influenced by the gravitational potential of a source object. We establish that to determine the influence of a source object like the Earth on a tiny particle, we must calculate a complex matrix representation of the Hamiltonian, taking into account the particle's mass and its effect on both the particle's position in space and its motion. We demonstrate the significance of accurately incorporating mass into the particle description by identifying an error in a well-known article and outlining the correct calculation. We conclude that without precise calculations based on the mass-dependent wave function of a particle, it is impossible to accurately determine the influence of a source object like the Earth on a tiny particle. This project aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the intersection between quantum mechanics and general relativity. We hope this project inspires young physicists to investigate further the fascinating relationship between quantum mechanics and gravitational physics. We also hope this project inspires the next generation of physicists to investigate more effectively the profound connection between quantum mechanics and gravitational physics. We conclude by emphasizing the importance of precise calculations in understanding how gravitational forces affect quantum systems, especially in the context of mass-dependent particles. We rely on the mass-dependent wave function of a particle to determine its behavior correctly. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end models with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to enhance the speech-text mapping, thereby improving the entire recognition process. Our proposed method, termed CycleER, has been extensively tested on various benchmark datasets and has produced consistently superior results, achieving a 4.6% absolute improvement on the Wall Street Journal dataset and a 3.2% on the LibriSpeech dataset compared to the baseline models. Moreover, CycleER has yielded notable performance gains when integrated with the Transducer model on the LibriSpeech dataset, surpassing a pre-trained Convolution-Absolute-Poisson (CAP) model by 5.4% in terms of recognition accuracy. Overall, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition using the CycleER method. It is expected that this technique will have a significant positive impact on the speech community in reducing the need for large speech-text paired data in model training. One of the most significant issues in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the domain shift problem, which leads to poor results in target domains.  Previous approaches mainly concentrated on minimizing the domain shift between training and testing datasets, however, they did not fully take into account the domain differences.  On the other of hand, some studies have focused solely on object detection and overlooked the domain shift issue.  In this paper, we present a novel bottom-up strategy called U2 together with a domain adaptive training method, to address the domain shift problem in pedestrian detection.  The U2 network is specifically designed to adapt to target domains by utilizing unified object representation.  Inspired by the top-down object relationship, U2 leverages object spatial pyramid and inter-object relations to learn an object representation that is more domain-adaptive.  In addition, U2 incorporates a domain adaptive training method called Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to minimize the domain shift between training and testing datasets.  Our experiments show that U2 achieves a significant mean average precision increase of 6.2% and 4.5% compared to state-of-the-art models on caltech and tidalester datasets respectively. This model is further validated by demonstrating its compatibility with real-world data through parameter adjustment. Furthermore, a stochastic gradient algorithm is derived for the simultaneous optimization of the model parameters and a simulation-based comparison with alternative distributions is conducted. The proposed distribution is found to outperform geometric and lognormal distributions in modeling the lower bounds of multiplicative stochastic processes. Finally, the developed model is validated by examining its convergence in sequences of independent and identically distributed random variables, where the finding that the model converges to a lognormal distribution in the limit, along with a corresponding sufficient condition for this convergence, is presented. Ultimately, the practical applicability of the model is demonstrated through a case study involving income inequality over time in various countries. The study reveals that the model provides a satisfactory fit to the data on income inequality during the last three decades in the United States, while also indicating that income inequality in recent years has approached lognormal behavior. In contrast, the model fails to accurately capture income trends in Brazil and India during the specified time period. This investigation highlights the utility of the proposed distribution as a statistical tool for characterizing lower bound multiplicative stochastic processes and their applicability to the study of income inequality over time. This protocol involves taking measurements on a family of modified Clifford circuits where each layer uses a randomly chosen gate. These protocols have been proven to effectively reproduce the capabilities of near-optimal measurement schemes. We explored the average performance of DRMs, both with random and predetermined gate sequences, in relation to the number of gates, using a method for approximating their output probabilities based on the matrix representation of the associated Clifford groups. This average performance metric can be seen as a non-orthogonal Rayleigh quotient. This finding validates the use of DRMs as a practical solution for optimal measurement schemes. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between near-optimal measurement schemes and the complexity of optimizing their performance. The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To address this challenge, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training fully convolutional neural network models on subsets of various sizes from a total dataset, each model undergoes a different image enhancement while its performance is compared to a baseline model trained without such augmentations on the entire dataset. Our results indicate that using rotations as an image enhancement yields the most significant reductions in labelled data required for the models to match the baseline performance. Additionally, combining rotations and brightness adjustments significantly lowers the necessity for labelled data. Ultimately, these findings suggest that incorporating multiple image enhancement techniques can substantially decrease the need for annotated images in chest X-ray pneumonia detection by semantic segmentation. It is observed that using rotations alone allows the models to reach the baseline performance with the dataset that is 4 times smaller than the baseline. Furthermore, applying rotations and brightness adjustments results in the models reaching the baseline performance with the dataset that is 8 and 16 times smaller respectively. This approach has proven effective in adapting an existing image captioning model to generate captions in multiple styles and domains. The method also facilitates the advancement of traditional image captioning by leveraging pre-trained language models to produce more detailed and semantically rich outputs. Experimental results demonstrate that our flexible image captioning system outperforms current state-of-the-art models across all proposed tasks. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish legal frameworks and ethical guidelines for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in literature have failed to consider the underlying causal mechanisms, largely due to the complex nature of many real-world examples. This study propounds a novel approach to harmonization by leveraging causal models, which are capable of handling intricate, transitive scenarios. A case in point is the phenomenon of Tesla vehicles accidentally driving into the ocean. According to our definition, an autonomous system causes harm to a person if another system causes harm to the person through the exercise of the autonomous system's capabilities. This definition hinges on the specificity of the causal link between the two systems, which can be established using causal models that incorporate shared variables. Ultimately, our proposed concept of harm is demonstrated to be both analytically and practically relevant. Furthermore, while previous definitions of harm are often non-transitive, ours shows that transitivity can, in fact, provide necessary legal and ethical clarity in specific scenarios, thus offering a valuable tool for decision-makers. Ultimately, our framework bears resemblance to existing notions of harm in social science research, particularly those that emphasize social inequalities and power dynamics. By developing an action-based framework for harm, we are able to identify instances where an autonomous system causes harm to a person by making a harmful action, such as accelerating, a prerequisite for the person's goal, as identified by the system's built-in objectives. This study offers a significant advancement in understanding autonomous systems by providing a new perspective on the relationship between these systems, harm, and transmissibility. It also paves the way for further research into the intersection of these topics, contributing to a broader understanding of autonomous systems. Interestingly, our definition of harm stands in contrast to existing concepts of agency and transmissibility in the social science literature, particularly those that emphasize intentional action and direct causality. By distinguishing our approach from established notions of harm, we are able to shed light on the limitations of existing definitions and provide a more nuanced understanding of autonomous systems. Moreover, our definition of harm is notable for its focus on the underlying causal mechanisms, as well as its ability to identify instances of harm that involve multiple, interconnected systems. Speech-to-text translation, a complex task that connects spoken words to written words in multiple languages, typically relies on large datasets that are time-consuming and costly to gather. One recent technique to overcome this problem is zero-shot translation, which uses models to translate speech without explicit training data through association with written texts. In this research, we focus on speech-to-text translation and reveal that existing large-scale models often produce errors due to inaccuracies in representing speech-to-text translation. We propose a new method, called Speech-to-Text Translation Projection, which uses a two-stage process to map speech representations to a unified speech-to-text space. Our STTP method achieves significant improvements in zero-shot translation accuracy across multiple languages, outperforming current best practices by 3-6% in cross-lingual speech translation tasks. Our code and models are publicly available. 

Key contributions:
- We identify the root cause of existing large-scale models' failure in zero-shot translation.
- We introduce a new method, Speech-to-Text Translation Projection (STTP), which improves zero-shot translation accuracy.
- Our method, STTP, is shown to outperform current best practices by 3-6% in zero-shot translation.

- Speech-to-text translation

- Cross-lingual learning
- Multilingual learning.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate peak demand forecasts is crucial, making multimodal probability models suitable candidates due to their capacity to capture sudden changes and peak variations. However, traditional multimodal probability models are less effective in the context of energy forecasting due to their difficulty in handling future data streams and peak parameter estimation. This paper presents a novel approach to modeling energy consumption with peak demand using probabilistic models, where peak demand is represented as a random variable following a normal distribution. By employing Bayesian methods for model integration, a dynamic model that combines forecasted peak demand from individual customers and aggregated consumption is developed. This approach achieves accurate predictions by complementing a Bayesian linear model, which forecasts aggregated consumption, with a Potts model, which predicts peak demand. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to established forecasting methods, such as ARIMA, ARBN, and Google Trends, both in estimating peak demand and aggregated consumption. The model's versatility in handling data on a large scale, with a small number of parameters, makes it suitable for near real-time high resolution load forecasting. Additionally, the paper investigates the relationship between estimated parameters and specific customer characteristics, such as building types and energy prices, highlighting the model's ability to provide building-level estimates of energy consumption during direct marketing campaigns. The model's performance in peak demand forecasting indicates that it can effectively identify potential peak generators within a network, which is essential for peer-to-peer energy trading and direct marketing strategies. The approach presented in this paper represents a significant advancement in peak demand estimation at a high resolution, which is essential for managing energy distribution efficiently in the near future. The model's ability to provide accurate forecasts at a high resolution, combined with its adaptability, makes it suitable for a wide range of energy distribution systems. The proposed method is open source, allowing researchers to replicate the findings, validate the approach, and expand its applications to other energy-related forecasting tasks. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorders. However, certain pathological conditions such as vertebral fractures, tumors, and degenerative diseases (e.g. degenerative spondylolisthesis, scoliosis, stenosis, etc.) make it difficult to distinguish between vertebrae and lesions or bony growths. In cases of degenerative spinal changes, the distinction between adjacent vertebrae disc spaces is also challenging. This paper presents an innovative approach to automatically identify and localize vertebrae, taking into account the presence of lesions and taking into consideration the distance between disc spaces. The proposed method has been developed using transverse, sagittal, and coronal MRI views from the patient's bottom to top, incorporating lesion detection to bypass manual vertebrae labeling, thereby facilitating automatic positioning of the spinal disc spaces. The approach is evaluated on 30 patients with spinal degenerations, 20 with vertebral fractures, and 10 with tumors, demonstrating effective performance on the complete lumbar spine (from L1 to L5). The research is significant in that it enables accurate automatic positioning of the spinal disc spaces for patients with various pathological conditions. The proposed method has achieved mean position errors of 2.9, 3.9, and 4.3 vertebral levels for transverse, sagittal, and coronal views respectively, indicating a promising outcome for patients with different pathological conditions. Within an extremely high level of ionization, the electron behaves as a continuous wave propagating through space outside the barrier, where it encounters a rotating wave of confined polaritons inside the barrier. Instead, the electron's short-term motion is influenced by the polariton's frequency only in the vicinity of the barrier, where an inelastic process occurs upon matching energies. We've developed an innovative variational quantum algorithm that determines whether a given quantum circuit produces separable states. Our algorithm, variational separability verifier (VSV), leverages the potential of variational quantum algorithms to tackle the problem of determining separability in high-dimensional quantum states, where it has been shown that certain criteria can effectively detect separability with minimal error. However, these criteria are typically applied in an optimal manner to specific families of states. VSV is based on a variational optimization of these criteria and demonstrates effectiveness in distinguishing separable and inseparable states. Our experiments show that VSV is capable of achieving high accuracy in distinguishing separable and inseparable states for small qubit systems. Moreover, VSV's performance is even superior to a variant of the quantum state discriminant (QSD) algorithm on certain tasks, and it has the added benefit of allowing for a free and explicit evaluation of its accuracy. Our results suggest that VSV could be employed as a pre-processing tool to identify circuits producing separable states, thus facilitating the implementation of quantum algorithms that require separability. Constructing the matching cost is a crucial step in estimating light field depth but has received insufficient attention. The costs generated can significantly impact the accuracy and speed of depth estimation, making it a critical component of the light field stereo algorithm. A novel cost constructor, designed with simplicity and speed in mind, is introduced in this paper to outperform existing constructions, particularly by utilizing a redefined measure that leverages hyper-spectral cues to enhance depth estimation while requiring minimal computational resources. When integrated with the light field stereo algorithm, this constructor achieves enhanced performance on 7M, SLF, NPLF, PMLF, NLNeRF, TLR, and TLR$^3$ datasets and datasets from the new challenge without increasing computational cost, boasting a direct improvement of up to 2.0 times. This study utilizes the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first discovered by Fokas and Lenells in 2007. This system of equations is a well-known example of a completely integrable equations model. Our analysis reveals one- and two-soliton solutions for Fokas-Lenells equations through the use of two relevant dark soliton solutions. Furthermore, two-soliton solutions exhibit a remarkable phenomenon of reflected and transmitted waves when a medium of zero value is encountered. This phenomenon aligns with previously documented results. Additionally, our research confirms that Fokas-Lenells equations also produce one- and two-soliton solutions. Notably, two-soliton solutions exhibit distinct behavior in positive and negative frequency states, yielding four unique solutions. This is in addition to known results for Fokas-Lenells equations. A detailed explanation of the method used to obtain these results is also provided. Lastly, this study serves as a foundation for further research into the Fokas-Lenells equations, enabling the derivation of high-order rogue wave solutions. A separate study is dedicated to obtaining these high-order solutions.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results. By embedding these theories within a regulated double field theory framework, it also calculates their corresponding Tulliview limits, which have actions that can be simply interpreted. Embedding these alternative gravity theories within a regulated double field framework provides a straightforward understanding of their G-causal nature. It further demonstrates that some of these theories exhibit features beyond mere non-Riemannian covariance. By studying these theories within this framework, it provides insights into their behavior at the level of their motion equations and action principles. It also sheds light on their properties in the Tulliview limit. It is hoped that these results lay the foundation for future investigations into these theories' physical properties within the Tulliview limit. As the demands on home WiFi networks continue to rise with the emergence of next-generation technologies such as virtual reality and high-quality video streaming, improving network performance has become a pressing concern. To address this challenge, we present a novel dual-beam WiFi technology, referred to as Dual-Beam WiFi (DBM), designed for indoor use within 802.11ax networks. By utilizing two separate transmission beams, DBM achieves more precise directionality and enhances signal stability while minimizing interference from external sources. We develop an optimal beam training strategy, referred to as Dual-Beam Index Bootstrapping Protocol (DBIBP), tailored to the DBM architecture to efficiently identify the most suitable beam pair to maximize throughput. Our simulation results, carried out using a MatLab simulator, demonstrate that DBIBP achieves an average throughput increase of an order of magnitude over its initial benchmark variant. Moreover, DBIBP was found to outperform its primary competitor, Primary Metastree Search (PMS), by nearly two orders of magnitude. Our comprehensive analysis highlights that DBIBP's efficiency stems from its reduced number of channel sampling instances and beam pair combinations compared to PMS. Our research results serve as a foundation for further investigations into the design of wireless networks, including optimization techniques, simulation tools, and wireless applications. Our proposed DBIBP algorithm, having been implemented in open source, is intended to facilitate future DBM-based system design studies. Our code is available for public access at: https://github.com/AMRumbaugh/DBM-Design. Our research contribution includes a comprehensive understanding of the DBM architecture and its associated design complexities, as well as a quantitative analysis of the DBM's performance characteristics. Our results indicate that DBM possesses a design complexity similar to that of conventional 802.11 WiFi networks but exhibits performance characteristics distinct from them. Our results show that DBM can achieve a network throughput capacity roughly an order of magnitude higher than its conventional WiFi counterpart under similar network conditions. Our experiments reveal that DBM can effectively support a variety of wireless applications, such as high-speed data transfers, while conventional WiFi networks are generally unable to support such applications reliably.
